Probably not. The issue isn't that equities are bad at 56, but that 100% in one fund removes every buffer right before the period when losses hurt most.

The main risk is sequence of returns. The S&P 500 fell about 49% in 2000-02 and about 57% in 2007-09, and it was roughly flat in nominal terms from 2000 to 2009. A drop like that at 60 means either selling low to fund living expenses or working years longer. At 30 you'd have time to recover, but at 56 you may not.

There's also concentration beyond the stock-only issue. The index is US large-cap only, and its top 10 holdings are now a large share of it, roughly a third or more. You get no bonds or cash, no international exposure, and no small or mid caps.

The strongest case for your idea is that retirement can last 30+ years, so you need growth, and holding too little equity carries its own risk of outliving your money. If a pension, Social Security, or a spouse's income will cover your essential expenses, you can take more equity risk. A high equity allocation is defensible. Many people your age hold about 60-80% stocks, and target-date funds for a 2035-2040 retirement sit in that range.

What would change my answer: guaranteed income covering your spending, flexibility to delay retirement, or a drawdown tolerance you've actually tested. A sensible test is whether you could watch the balance fall 40-50% and not sell.

If this money is in a taxable account rather than a 401(k) or IRA, selling to move into the fund can trigger capital gains tax. Within a tax-advantaged account, there's no tax cost to rebalancing.

If you share your current allocation, target retirement age, and other income sources, I can give a more specific read. A fee-only fiduciary advisor is worth a one-time consult for a decision this large.
